x.A: Kinesis Data Streams needs a consumer to deliver the log data to OpenSearch, so you'd write and run that consumer.
x.B: VPC Flow Logs go to a CloudWatch Logs log group, and Kinesis Data Firehose can stream the logs from the log group to OpenSearch Service in near real time, with no code to maintain.
x.C: VPC Flow Logs can't be sent to a CloudTrail trail, because CloudTrail records API activity.
x.D: Flow logs can't be sent to a CloudTrail trail, so this is invalid, even though Firehose is the right delivery service.

x.A: A managed node group of Spot Instances is the cheapest, and since the development cluster is used infrequently to test resiliency, interruptions are acceptable. EKS manages all the nodes.
x.B: Keeping an On-Demand node group alongside Spot costs more, which isn't needed for a development cluster used rarely.
x.C: A self-built Auto Scaling group means the company manages the nodes, but the cluster must manage all the nodes, which managed node groups do.
x.D: On-Demand Instances cost more than Spot for a cluster that is used infrequently and can tolerate interruptions.

x.A: SSE-S3 keys are managed entirely by S3, so the company can't control creating, rotating, or disabling them.
x.B: A KMS customer managed key lets the company create, rotate (including automatic rotation), and disable the key, and SSE-KMS applies it to the S3 objects with little effort.
x.C: An AWS managed key is created and rotated by AWS, so the company can't control its lifecycle.
x.D: Downloading, encrypting on EC2, and uploading is a lot of manual work and not necessary with SSE-KMS.

x.A: S3 Object Lock enforces retention so the backups can't be deleted or overwritten during the 30 days.
x.B: Versioning isn't needed for retention and would keep older versions around, which makes automatic deletion harder.
x.C: A default retention period of 30 days on the bucket applies to all new objects, so each backup is protected for 30 days.
x.D: A lifecycle policy can't protect objects from deletion. It only transitions or expires them.
x.E: A lifecycle rule that expires objects after 30 days deletes the backups automatically once the retention ends.
x.F: Tagging doesn't enforce retention by itself, and it needs the backup solution to be changed.

x.A: DataSync with a location for the destination S3 bucket and the EFS file system, set to transfer only changed data, copies new files continuously and overwrites only when the source changes. It's managed and needs little work.
x.B: A Lambda function with EFS mounted needs custom code, and large files may hit Lambda limits, so it's more overhead.
x.C: Transferring all data copies and overwrites every file each time, which doesn't meet the requirement to overwrite only changed files.
x.D: An EC2 instance with a custom sync script means managing a server and code.

x.A: A customer managed KMS key lets the company control rotation (enable, disable, or manually rotate), and encrypting the EBS volumes with it needs very little work.
x.B: AWS managed keys are rotated automatically by AWS, and you can't configure their rotation. The company needs control.
x.C: A key with imported key material must be rotated manually, which is more operational work.
x.D: AWS owned keys are managed by AWS and aren't visible in your account, so you can't control rotation.

x.A: An IAM policy limits users to creating encrypted EBS volumes, and AWS Config detects unencrypted ones. Systems Manager Automation can remediate them automatically, so noncompliant resources are fixed with little overhead.
x.B: KMS manages keys, and building detection and remediation with Lambda and EventBridge means custom code to maintain.
x.C: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3 and doesn't detect unencrypted EBS volumes.
x.D: Inspector scans for vulnerabilities and doesn't evaluate EBS encryption.

x.A: A web tier in an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB improves resiliency with no application changes.
x.B: A database in an Auto Scaling group behind an NLB doesn't keep a single MySQL database's data consistent across instances, so this isn't a valid design.
x.C: RDS Multi-AZ for MySQL provides automatic failover for the database, and since it's MySQL, the application changes are minimal.
x.D: Moving the web tier to Lambda needs the application code to be rewritten, which goes against minimizing changes.
x.E: Migrating to DynamoDB would require a major application change.

x.A: CloudFront edge locations cache content, but you can't deploy applications into a VPC extended to a CloudFront edge location.
x.B: AWS Local Zones extend a Region's VPC to a location closer to users, and they provide single-digit millisecond latency for applications that can't run in the nearby Region.
x.C: Regional edge caches are part of CloudFront's caching layer, and you can't extend a VPC to them.
x.D: Wavelength Zones are for 5G mobile edge applications inside telecom networks, not general web applications.

x.A: A custom endpoint distributes connections among instances but doesn't pool connections, so Lambda could still overload the database with many connections.
x.B: RDS Proxy pools and shares database connections so Lambda invocations don't overload the database. The Lambda functions must be in the VPC to reach the private RDS Proxy endpoint.
x.C: A custom endpoint doesn't pool connections, and a function outside the VPC can't reach a private database.
x.D: RDS Proxy is right, but functions outside a VPC can't reach a private proxy endpoint.

x.A: Peering VPCs and VPNs to each VPC grows complex with more accounts and VPCs, since peering isn't transitive.
x.B: A VPN software appliance on EC2 is a single point of failure and has to be managed and scaled by hand.
x.C: A transit gateway is a central hub. VPCs attach to it with VPC attachments, and the on-premises locations connect with VPN attachments, so new connections are simple to add and it scales.
x.D: Direct Connect to a central VPC with peering to others isn't transitive, so each new VPC needs more connections, which increases administration.

x.A: Deploying a SageMaker model and endpoint requires ML skills, which the company doesn't have.
x.B: Training a SageMaker model needs ML expertise, which the company lacks.
x.C: A Lambda function calling SageMaker endpoints still depends on a SageMaker model that must be built.
x.D: A Lambda function with a function URL that calls a Forecast predictor gives predictions based on the inputs, without ML experience.
x.E: Amazon Forecast trains a predictor from historical time-series data in S3 automatically, without ML expertise.

x.A: Creating users for each account and custom IAM policies per group means managing permissions separately in each account.
x.B: Attaching managed policies to each user individually doesn't scale and is manual for every new hire.
x.C: Users in IAM Identity Center are put in developer and administrator groups. Permission sets define each group's permissions, and are assigned to the groups for the accounts. New hires only need to be added to the right group.
x.D: Assigning permission sets to individual users and adding extra IAM permissions in specific accounts is hard to manage as the team grows.

x.A: API calls scheduled with Lambda means writing and maintaining code, and it isn't continuous.
x.B: Running API calls in a Fargate task means writing code and paying for a task, which is more operational work.
x.C: A tagging policy and manual encryption don't check encryption automatically and need a lot of manual effort.
x.D: An AWS Config managed rule evaluates whether EBS volumes are encrypted and flags those that aren't, with no code and little cost.

x.A: An access point simplifies managing access to a bucket and doesn't increase upload or download throughput.
x.B: Uploading to multiple buckets doesn't help throughput for a single file and complicates management.
x.C: Multipart uploads upload parts in parallel, which increases upload throughput for GB-sized files.
x.D: Fetching multiple byte ranges of an object in parallel increases download throughput to the EC2 instances.
x.E: S3 automatically scales by prefix, so random prefixes aren't needed anymore.

x.A: A Volume Gateway presents iSCSI volumes that attach to individual instances, so they aren't a shared file system with strong consistency across instances.
x.B: EFS is a shared file system with strong consistency, so any instance sees changes as soon as they're made.
x.C: An EBS volume attaches to a single instance (Multi-Attach works only in one AZ and has limits), so it can't be shared across AZs.
x.D: DataSync synchronizes on a schedule, so content isn't consistent as soon as changes occur.
x.E: S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency, and setting Cache-Control to no-cache with CloudFront ensures that new content is fetched from the origin right after changes.

x.A: A latency routing policy sends each user to the Region with the lowest latency, which gives the best performance. An A record (alias) points to the ALB.
x.B: Geolocation routing sends users by their location rather than lowest latency, which might not be the fastest.
x.C: A failover policy sends traffic to a secondary only when the primary fails, so it doesn't spread traffic for performance.
x.D: Geoproximity routing is based on distance and bias, not measured latency, and you can't use a CNAME at the zone apex for an ALB (use an alias).

x.A: An NLB doesn't improve availability across AZs by itself, and the embedded NoSQL database is still tied to each instance.
x.B: The database moves to DynamoDB, but the instances remain in a single AZ, so the application isn't highly available.
x.C: Instances across three AZs help, but keeping the embedded NoSQL database means running and maintaining the replication yourself.
x.D: The Auto Scaling group across three AZs makes the application highly available, and moving the embedded NoSQL database to DynamoDB (eventually consistent reads) is managed, so it needs the least operational overhead.

x.A: Sticky sessions keep a user on one instance, and the cart is lost if that instance fails, so it isn't preserved at all times.
x.B: ElastiCache for Redis caches catalog data with very low latency, and it keeps the shopping cart and session data in a highly available store with replication, so carts survive disconnects.
x.C: OpenSearch Service is a search and analytics engine and isn't the right place for session and cart data.
x.D: A single EC2 instance with EBS snapshots isn't highly available, and snapshots aren't continuous.

x.A: ElastiCache reduces requests to the microservices but doesn't make the application observable.
x.B: Container Insights collects metrics and logs from EKS clusters, and X-Ray traces requests between microservices, so performance issues can be identified.
x.C: CloudTrail records API calls, not performance or interactions between microservices.
x.D: Trusted Advisor gives general best-practice checks and doesn't show application performance.

x.A: ACM certificates are for TLS, not for encrypting data at rest, and certificate policies don't control who can read data in S3.
x.B: A bucket policy can't control KMS decryption. Decrypt permission is controlled by the KMS key policy.
x.C: A separate KMS key per customer encrypts the data server-side, and each key's policy denies decryption for everyone except the customer's IAM role, so company employees can't access the data.
x.D: ACM certificates don't protect data at rest, and there's no such thing as a public certificate policy controlling data access.

x.A: An Auto Scaling group doesn't give the instance public access, and a DNS record can't resolve to a group identifier.
x.B: An internet-facing ALB in a public subnet receives internet traffic and forwards it to the instance in the private subnet. The DNS record points to the ALB.
x.C: A NAT gateway allows outbound access from private subnets and doesn't accept inbound connections from the internet.
x.D: A private subnet instance has no public IP route, so security group changes and a public IP don't make it reachable and would break the security mandate.

x.A: EBS volumes can't be used with Fargate, and Multi-Attach has limits, so it doesn't work for sharing data.
x.B: EFS is a shared file system that Fargate pods can mount, and it's highly available across AZs with no capacity to manage. Registering it in a StorageClass lets all the containers share it.
x.C: EBS volumes can't be shared by multiple containers and aren't supported on Fargate for EKS.
x.D: Separate EFS file systems per AZ with a Lambda sync is unnecessary, because EFS already spans AZs.

x.A: EKS with self-managed nodes and EBS means managing servers and storage, which the company doesn't want.
x.B: ECS on Fargate runs containers without servers to manage, and an EFS volume is fully managed, persistent, shared storage that can be mounted in the containers.
x.C: S3 can't be mounted as a persistent volume in Fargate containers.
x.D: The EC2 launch type means managing the underlying EC2 instances, which the company wants to avoid.

x.A: Internal NLBs in each Region give targets that Global Accelerator can route to, and NLBs support both TCP and UDP.
x.B: ALBs support only HTTP and HTTPS, so they can't carry TCP and UDP game traffic.
x.C: Global Accelerator routes users over the AWS global network to the nearest healthy Regional endpoint, supporting TCP and UDP, with high availability and minimum latency.
x.D: Geolocation routing is DNS-based, so it doesn't offer the failover speed or optimal path of Global Accelerator.
